utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Guy-Smith, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tetaj, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith, who is counsel for the defendant Balaj. Please proceeded, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you a couple of questions concerning your military experience and your military understanding. From what I understand of your background, you joined the military pretty much as a young man and that was going to be your intended career sometime around 1978. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1974 I was a cadet. In 1978 I finished military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you were a cadet in 1974, it would be fair to say that it was your intention to have as your career a military career for your life; that's what you were planning on doing?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You remained in the military, and that's with the JNA, until what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1989, by the end of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at the time that you left the military, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as a matter of fact, was forced to resign from the JNA because I was an Albanian officer of career. The situation politically was such in the Yugoslav territories, so I was at that time captain of first rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to, if you could for the Chamber, I'd like to see if you can describe a couple of things. As a member of the military, were you issued a uniform when you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I had a uniform of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you, during the time that you were in the JNA, ever in need of ammunition or was there always sufficient ammunition for anything you wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army had a lot of weapons. It was an army which had good place in Europe and even of world level. We had every kind of weapons up to the most contemporary types of weapons including missiles, kind of weapons which a world-class army has.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that as a matter of fact by the time you were forced to resign from the Serbian army, that you were a participant in one of the most advanced armies in the world at the time, one of the most technically sophisticated armies at the time?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we thought that the Yugoslav Army was the third-biggest army in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, as a captain did you have responsibility for soldiers under you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, what if the witness would say no, that not be a huge surprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be shocking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, I take your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say, yes, it's true, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How many men were under your command when you were a captain of the first rank and you resigned from the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning it was a unit of artillery division. I was a commander of squad which had few soldiers because it was specialised in land artillery. So in terms of number, we had few soldiers than the other units because we had the technique which did some of the job. So at the moment when I was dismissed there was a division at the time, it had four units, so probably 130 up to 150 soldiers. This was the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And being specialised in the area of land artillery, I take it it would be fair to say that you were responsible for tanks. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was specialised for tanks -- not for tanks, less for tanks but for the system of armoured vehicles and also for land-to-land missile system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said there came a time when you had to resign, and I'd like to ask you some questions about what had occurred shortly before your resignation -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, could you please activate your microphone. It was my mistake, it was something on my priority button, which, as may be clear, I will never hardly ever use.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where I was going was this: By 1989, the Serbian parliament, to your knowledge, had limited the autonomy of Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could speak to you and tell you then that at that time we had officers of different nationalities, starting from 1980s all the officers of Albanian nationality were the targets of the Serbian army. So the first discrimination began. That happened, and the fact is many officers of the Yugoslav Army, there was a secret service of the state which did this. I belonged to a generation which graduated from the military academy and we were the first people, we were about 30 Albanians, the first batch of Albanian officers who graduated from this academy. So at that time there was a lot of people -- there were a lot of people who were interrogated, people who were taken away from their houses. There were also other things which happened. As a matter of fact, many Albanian officers and soldiers became the target. Many soldiers -- Albanian soldiers came back from the army with injuries. It was an unenviable situation for every Albanian which at the time wore the uniform of the Serbian army. That began when Tito died in early 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a secret service of the state which did this and with regard to the secret service of the state, is that the Serbian state that was involved in --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military. I, in fact, referred to the Yugoslav state and the secret service of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The secret service that existed at that time, when you were still in the army, did you personally be called to task for purpose -- because you were Albanian and asked questions about what your political leanings were and what your intentions were as regards the Serbians themselves?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was questioned, mostly because I was an officer of Albanian nationality, and also because in 1980s there were the first demonstration in university in Pristina. So every Albanian officer who was in the Yugoslav Army was subjected to interrogation by the secret service of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you decided to resign, you then got a job working ultimately in education - is that true - that was in, I believe, 1992 -- or I'm sorry, it was sometime after 1990.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you. When I left the army I went to Strumica. I had my house there, so I went back to my homeland. The situation in the homeland was such that I needed employment. So after a competition in Rilindja, I competed for the job as chief of radio and television of Kosovo. I was admitted. So I was admitted and given the job as the first chief of the radio and television of Pristina as the first Albanian chief in the autonomous province of Kosovo. However, unfortunately, on the very first day I was admitted, despite my preparations, on that very day the Serbian forces took over the television building so I have not a single day of work and career in this job. Afterwards in Rilindja stuff was dismissed, so another newspaper appeared, Bujku. I competed then for a job in the secondary school in Klina. I was admitted and I began teaching in that school in Klina as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After that attempt working in the television industry, you ultimately got a job for a limited period of time in a secondary school as a teacher; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at the time you were working as a teacher in the secondary school, was the educational system of apartheid already in place, and by that I mean that Albanians and Serbians were taught in two separate systems with two separate languages?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True. We were in the same building but we were in true different classes. The Albanian pupils were the majority; the other were the minority. The director was actually imposed on us. He was imposed on us by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ultimately your experience working as an educator also stopped and that was as a result of the fact that you refused to follow the Serbian-imposed programme of education?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True. I and my colleagues wanted that the curriculum should be in Albanian language. We wanted to have programme of Albanian status, but we had a lot of problems. So after a short period of time, we were even removed from the building which was the property of the Albanian people, the majority. So then the classes began to be held in all kinds of makeshift facilities in private houses in Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say after a short period of time you were even removed from the building, who removed you from the building?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The violent director, together with the police, the local police of the Serbian. They told us that only those who accepted Serbian curriculum would be allowed to continue to remain in the schools. So no pupil was allowed to go through the main gate or a teacher wasn't allowed to enter through the main gate of the school. So we were forced to choose another system in order to continue the education. So at that time in Kosova every house was turned into a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you left that job you were ultimately arrested, I believe, in September of 1993, accused of terrorist activities and imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. True. After my dismissal from school, we went to the villages. I lived in a village. It was far away. We had no money. I was arrested somewhere on 29th of September, 1993. They accused me of preparing a system for secession and for seeking to set up a military organisation to separate Kosova from Yugoslavia. These were the charges on basis of the Serbian penal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned to us but a few moments ago that while you were in the military the state secret service interrogated you because you were Albanian?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is your experience in 1993, were you once again interrogated by the state secret service with regard to their suspicions of you being involved in activities against the state?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested on 29th of September. They kept me for three days and three nights in SUP of Peje. The people who interrogated me were civilians. They were people sent from Belgrade. They had military experience also. So they asked me questions which were related to my activity in the army and during the time since I had left the army. True what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were being interrogated in 1993, were you shown your file; and by that I mean were you shown a file that included all of the both, I'd say, you know, factual as well as surveillance information that they had about your life from the time that you were in the military up to and through 1993, when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not show me any file. They asked me a lot of questions about all kind of things. They accused me of organising a formation of 1.200 soldiers in Dukagjin Plain. However, when I appeared in the court, they could not bring any evidence about these 1.200 people, they could not bring any witness to show and prove that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were being interrogated in 1993, did they mention to you at that time names of other individuals they believed that you were working with or conspiring with against the state?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us who some of those people were that they accused you of working with and conspiring with against the state at the time?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehmet Bojki, who was member of the Democratic League of Kosova and he was an experienced captain of Territorial Defence of Decan; Ibrahim Ukhaxhaj from Decan. They asked me about the defence minister at that time Hajzer Hajzeraj, who was the minister of the autonomous province of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were convicted, you went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Pardon. This was the minister for the autonomous province or provinces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the minister of the autonomous province of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add here that in the 1980s Kosova took part and was represented like all republics in the Yugoslav system; however, in the military system the autonomous province had the same Territorial Defence as the other republics. However, in 1980, upon an order of the General Staff of Yugoslav Army, people were dismissed from work. The system of Territorial Defence was abolished. So nobody was anymore in charge. This was done only in Kosova. There was some kind of inspection on the part of people from Yugoslavia. They came there to check the situation in every municipality, in every barracks. So Kosova was stripped of the Territorial Defence system, which until that time it was of the same level as the armed forces of Yugoslavia. So what they did, they did it only in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the net effect of the -- Kosovo being stripped of the Territorial Defence system was that there was no standing group of men and women who were able to defend Kosovo, correct, an organised group?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Until 1980 we had the system. We had people of career who worked in the Territorial Defence system; however, this system was abolished. The same thing was done with the schools. So the weapons from that time was taken over the army. The Yugoslav Army was one part and then the Territorial Defence system was also a component of the Yugoslav forces. So the Territorial Defence system, together with the units, together with the ammunition and the military equipment, all of this was taken away from us and it was put in the hands of the Yugoslav Army. So this happened in 1980. From that time, there was no longer any Territorial Defence system in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I want to move up to 1998, and as I understand the evidence you've given thus far, you were at that time in your village in Donja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in March, as we've heard, there was an attack on the Haradinaj family compound, which you not only heard but you saw parts of; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During that period of time in your village, was there any form of or group of people who were trying to deal with defending the village in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally had military experience in the -- there were 41 villages in Decan. The people were stripped of jobs, were stripped of education, were stripped of Territorial Defence. People were jobless. People at that time left the country altogether, they felt insecure. So at that time we discussed about how we could set up a system. We thought about how we could set up -- set up a defence. Of course this was only theoretical talking because we had no means to do that, because at that time the war broke out in Slovenia, in Croatia, in Bosnia. So these were the big concerns and we thought what we should do here at home to defend ourselves. So in a most secret way we discussed all this. The state secret was very active so it was difficult. So we discussed and thought about how we could set up a system in order to be capable of coping with an eventual attack and how the population would behave in face of such an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned the state secret was very active, and I take it by that you mean the state secret service was active during that time?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say they were active, what were they doing at that time? Were they arresting young men and women for alleged terrorist acts during that time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of what time, Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- are we speaking of? Because the witness answered the question before in a very broad way, including the whole decade of the 1990s, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll make it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- referring to Slovenia and Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll make it more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Tetaj. For the purposes of the question I'm asking, I'm dealing right now with the months of February and March, during that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- was the state secret service involved in arresting young men and women for alleged terrorist acts, and that would be for 1998?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not taken for terrorists but for political reasons. So people were interrogated. They were brought to facilities where they were interrogated. There was harassment. This was done for political reasons. They were asking whether people had weapons. They asked us whether you had -- we had a gun, et cetera. So I would also like to add - which I think is of importance - in my municipality in Decan, there was a small minority of Serbs and Montenegrins; however, these people had all the posts in Decan municipality. So even if somebody had -- had followed a course for a waiter, he was the chief of finance in the municipality. So people without education, they had all these posts. So on the other hand, the population, people who were intellectuals, who had education, they were left jobless. This happened in the municipality and this could be said so for the posts of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The meetings that you were having in your village, how many people were involved in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My village is a big one -- in fact, it's rather -- rather small comparatively. Each household - and I'm talking about the last stage - there was a volunteer coming from each household. So in total, we could talk about 30 households, 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you said you're talking about the last stage, could you give us a time-frame in which you're dealing with the last stage in which you received volunteers from 30 households, so that's 30 people.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time when the -- the operational staff for the Dukagjin region was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be before the first meeting that you had that you were invited to with Ramush Haradinaj and others?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up until then there were some five, six, seven people, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At that time, when there were five, six, seven, before the May meeting, was your village at that time attacked by the Serb forces, either the MUP or SUP?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time we were organised on the basis of cells. One was in the upper Luka. At the time we were organised on the basis of a system of cells in certain points, key points, which would not allow the Serb forces to move in. Our village was a bit more internal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to now move to discuss Faik, I believe his last name is Gecaj. Is that a correct pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gecaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Faik Gecaj was somebody who lived in your village; true?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in my village, but he mostly lived in Germany and the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He is the -- he is the individual who brought to your village a series of light weapons and a uniform for you; right?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is something that he did independently - and by "independently," I mean it was a village decision to obtain these weapons and I take it his getting you a uniform was a personal decision on his part?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his own voluntary decision, but it wasn't his initiative. It was the initiative of the village to send someone across to bring us enough weapons for the first stage so that that cell in the village could have weapons, be equipped with weapons for self-defense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that the only person who had a uniform I believe during the entire time that you remained in Kosovo until you left in September was yourself, for your village?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true. The rest were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The other people who fought with you, some were volunteers and some were part of the KLA structure. Is that a fair statement? And I'm only referring now to your village.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, was there any way of making a distinction between somebody who was a volunteer and somebody who was part of the KLA army? And I'm referring now to the issue of uniforms. And what I'm trying to understand is: Would it be fair to say that a lot of people wore whatever they had available to them in terms of clothing to go fight? Some people wore camouflage, shirt or pants if they had it...

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to make a clarification. Look, for the moment at that time, not only those who had a uniform, not only those who had weapons, not only those who were daring, but also young, old, young and old, in one way or another supported the KLA. They felt in the moral aspect to be members of that army, but they had no weapons, they had no uniform. Every corner, every bit of Kosovo felt as part of the KLA, including women and children, but the reality was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Those people who did attempt to clothe themselves in some kind of uniform often would wear a pair of black pants and a black shirt, and right now I'm talking about in your village during the summer of 1998. That was one of the ways of identifying themselves as being in support of the KLA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people who did that, a country member exactly, but it was a great wish to have a weapon, to have a uniform, so that they could be identified as member of an army, a member of the KLA. So everybody wanted -- but each and every one individually were trying to do their own thing to achieve this status.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Some people, for example, do you know an individual by the name of Mete Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mete Krasniqi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He wore a black uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was part of the police; true?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he called himself, but to this day I have no idea who oriented him to do that but it was his own will. But all those who were wearing such uniforms, they had an idea of establishing such an entity; but it was his own personal initiative that he did earlier before everything happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the entity that Mete Krasniqi was involved in, do you know other people who worked with him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with Mete Krasniqi at the time it was Din Krasniqi, a doctor, and I also know that Faton Mehmeti was in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did they, too, wear black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Faton Mehmeti was wearing a camouflage uniform. The doctor had no uniform. He was in civilian clothing, I'm talking about Din Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mete Krasniqi is an individual who travelled extensively through the four subzones that you've identified for us, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if I understand your evidence, he operated on his own personal initiative; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I've seen him, I saw him moving around. I can say that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not he carried handcuffs with him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as far as handcuffs are concerned, I'm not aware of that. He carried a weapon. He travelled in a car. In my village, in my subzone and in subzone 4 there were many things about Mete Krasniqi. As I said, he was from Vranoc, but most of his life he lived in Peje. Initially -- well, before. He was not know as Mete Krasniqi but he was most popularly known by the name of Mete Vranoci. Mete Krasniqi was his family name, but he was known as Mete Vranoci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your contact with Mete Krasniqi, did he ever discuss with you lists of people that he was interested in?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first contact that I had with him was in September, when we withdrew to the Bjeshka of Rugova, and he was a civilian then, he had no uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've -- I'm noticing, Your Honour, that on line 22, the witness said subzone 4, I don't know whether he misspoke himself or whether there's a mis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any doubt, please ask the witness, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your subzone was subzone -- what was your subzone, subzone 3 or subzone 4?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine was number 3, but I said that on the side of Bistrica in subzone 4 he was seen circulating around that area. And it was along the valley of Baran that he was travelled. But my subzone - and we're talking about subzones here - was number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you met Mete Krasniqi in September and he was a civilian then, was that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my clarification, just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He left [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Tetaj, I think you testified that Mete Krasniqi was wearing a black uniform. You said you -- the first contact you had with him was in September. Could you tell us whether you did see him wearing a black uniform before September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was moving around, travelling in a car. I haven't -- I haven't met him to stop and talk, but I've seen him driving his car in black uniform. He called himself as of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps one more question on this matter. You said you didn't stop him, you didn't meet him. How did you become aware that he said he called himself as of the military police? Is that what you heard from others? Did you hear that from Mr. Krasniqi himself? Could you please elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is other people came to me and asked me, How come that Mete Krasniqi is in a military police uniform? But people who knew him better than I did, they came to me. And they were surprised at the same time what was happening. Not to say that for the region he was a kind of suspicious person, and they knew him as Mete Vranoci rather than Mete Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yesterday when you were discussing the meeting in which various individuals were given various jobs, and that would be on the 23rd of June, 1998, with Mr. Emmerson you went through a number of names and discussed, among other things, what the actual capabilities were for the army and that in fact you were trying at some level to inform the population of what you were trying to do and what you hoped to do. One of the assignments that was made was an assignment that was made for the assistant for sabotage combat and the name there is the name Toger. It's something that Judge Orie, as a matter of fact, commented on. And I would like to talk to for a moment you about this particular assignment, which is the assistant for sabotage combat, if I might. In your military experience, could you explain to the Chamber what sabotage combat is.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am given the opportunity to explain, I -- I'm -- we are talking here about if a group, a diversionist group is sent to find out what's been happening on the enemy side and they do not carry out their tasks, then that is considered as sabotage. That's how I see it, the meaning of the word "sabotage." That means withdrawing from your duties without carrying them out, without having carried them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. In the situation -- in the situation that we're in, it would not make a great deal of sense, would it, to appoint somebody to a job like that - and by that I mean a job of withdrawing from your duties? And may I suggest to you that in this particular situation the idea was that whoever had that job - here, it's Toger - would go to Serb stations, police forces, or other military places and attempt to engage them in some form of military action or try to blow up or kill some of them?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, it's not clear to me, the question is not clear. But you explained it very well. If that's the role, that's how it should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at the time you were at the meeting and this particular assignment was made, can you -- as you sit here today, can you tell us what the purpose was for being the assistant to sabotage combat? If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know, and I'm not clear about which meeting we are talking about, I'm not clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What you do know, what you've told us is --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or I may not recall what went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's perfectly fair. That's fine. I -- and I thank you for your efforts. What you do know and what you have told us is that Togeri was the head of the Black Eagles, which was a group of young men, somewhere between 25 or 30 men; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've also told us that as you know, he was involved in actions - and by "he" I mean his unit - was involved in actions, that's battles, with the Serbs in a number of different villages; right?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the numbers you mentioned, and they were volunteers who were very daring, young people, and they were volunteers who joined Togeri completing this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... who had black clothes on?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing the black clothing, better to say, so that they could distinguish themselves from the rest. They had an insignia of the KLA on these dark clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could, if you could tell us the -- whether I'm correct when I mention the following areas, that these are places where the Black Eagles were involved in battles during the summer of 1998. Voksh?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Baballoq?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Prilep?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gramaqel?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Shaptej?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shaptej, about Shaptej, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Junik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there was -- the next village was not understood by the transcriber because the previous translation continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could we start on from Shaptej, next one would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Rastavice?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rastavice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Junik?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Carrabreg?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carrabreg, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no offensive there in Dubrava. It's near Gramaqel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think it's Sllup?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sllup, Lloqan, Voksh, they are located very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gllogjan, they -- they couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I also believe --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. I interrupted you. I do apologise. You said: "Gllogjan, they couldn't ..." And --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other forces there. They didn't need for -- they didn't need reinforcements there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Loxha?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loxhe, you are talking about Loxhe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your memory, are there other villages where the Black Eagles were involved in battles during the time that you were in Kosovo in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were the places which you mentioned. These were the places under heaviest attack. So in my opinion, I don't think of any other place. Of course there could be movements to different areas, but I don't remember other names other than the ones you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You earlier mentioned that the Black Eagles was comprised of a group of daring young men, and I'd like to talk to you for a moment about -- about that, because yesterday, among other things, when Mr. Re was discussing matters with you he had indicated that you had said that in your understanding when they were deployed to go fight, they never fought in groups of more than two or three. This was a very small unit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very small unit compared to the region, and a very, very small group was engaged in the actions, not the whole group. The daring people, the voluntary people who took part here did not simply want to carry black uniforms and carry one attack or another, but they wanted to be engaged in a training course for such actions. For example, they wanted to know how to use a weapon for a very brief period of time. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Black Eagles' responsibility was to come in and, among other things, reinforce the villages when the Serbs were attacking; right?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was its responsibility. In any case of Serbian action, its presence was a cause of pride for the people to see that the unit was there. So they -- the group gave its support. So if there was an attack against a village, like Carrabreg, Lluka, or Prilep, people always wanted to have the assistance, support, of the Black Eagles. It was moral support. The establishment of this unit was an act of moral support.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from being moral support, it was actually, in fact, true military support because these young men, Toger's unit, had weapons and training that allowed them to effectively fight against the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny this; it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Idriz Balaj was not from the area, was he?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to declare again openly, I had contacts with Idriz Balaj but I never knew him as Idriz Balaj. He can confirm it himself. I knew him as Toger and I knew that he did not come from that region. People did not know him in that region, and he also did not know the people of the surrounding villages. His name, Idriz Balaj, I read it and learned about it later, after I read some books on the KLA. Then I learned about the identity of the person of Idriz Balaj. But at the time, the way he spoke, I thought he was from Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. And I thank you -- I thank you for the answer. The man that you knew as Toger, not coming -- not coming from the area, this constituted somewhat of a double-edged sword for him, didn't it? And by that I mean he was doing good work, as you've just told us; his unit was supporting and helping the people, as you've told us; but he was a stranger and in the area in which you come from there were few strangers?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. That's true that he came there. He came there to defend the villages and the population of that region. And I'd like to thank him for doing that and possibly also in the name of -- he gave moral support to people, and in fact it's -- it was the hope that kept Togeri's unit and the people keeping on. People felt more secure when they were under attack from the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Part of the reality at the same time, however, was that if there was an effective defence, there would be a greater response by the Serbian army, wouldn't there? It would come in with more guns, more soldiers, more tanks?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Surely if the -- our forces grew in number, as they grew in number and techniques, also the Serbian forces grew in number. The same thing could be said about the reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... So a reality on the ground was that when Toger and the Black Eagles were present, there was fighting, there was death, and there was defence?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have put it up differently. There -- the Serbian forces continued less if the Black Eagle units were engaged. The action was shorter. Whether there is death or other casualties, nobody could really guess what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the action he took part, not only Toger but also other soldiers. Nobody thought that he would come back alive. This is how I would have put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think you've certainly put it better than I could because, among other things, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I could add something. Where we operated and where Toger operated, the Serbian forces were concentrated, they had their arsenal. I also showed you on the map where they were deployed in the region. We were under siege, so it was almost impossible for us to resort to big movements. So we did as few movements as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about one last matter, which is yesterday you confirmed in speaking to Mr. Re that you spoke with a young man in Tirana by the name of Astrit Berisha.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yesterday I mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You explained to us that Astrit Berisha was attempting to justify why he was not in Kosovo fighting, if I understood your testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You confirmed that Astrit Berisha told you that Toger killed every member of his unit that wanted to leave. That's what Astrit Berisha told you.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the withdrawal of FARK from Kosova is concerned, when this happened the people's hopes diminished. Therefore, Toger's units and the other units which remained in Dukagjini Plain were weakened, much weakened. They had also a lower morale. So the people who withdrew, they can confirm that he tried to justify why he withdrew, and I didn't think that what was said was true because if somebody comes to help me, if somebody comes to support me, I will try to do anything to ensure that everybody becomes Black Eagle. So he could not kill anybody. This is illogical. So I could say that he knew that I was an officer, I had participated. So he talked to me simply because he was weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were talking to the investigators from the Prosecutor's office about what Astrit Berisha told you, did you explain to them at that time that he was trying to justify the reasons that he fled the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Also, they didn't insist on asking me this. They asked me simply what I heard and with whom I had contacts. So then one question after another I came to that, what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you put a question to the witness on the small groups in which the Black Eagles operated. Do you happen to remember where exactly to find the source of that first testimony? You said two to three people. I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I'll give it to you in two seconds, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, Mr. Harvey, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Tetaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I am, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Harvey, who is counsel for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have four matters that I want to raise with you; I think they will all be short. The first concerns your visit to Jabllanice where you were asked on Monday by Mr. Re if Nazmi Brahimaj's house was the local KLA headquarters in Jabllanice. Do you remember him asking you that question?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was that your first -- sorry, no. You had visited Jabllanice in July -- sorry, the end of June, 23rd of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first time; this was the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you described that house as - at least the translation reads - "it's called a fort from our people here." Does the word "compound" sound like the right word to you? And I don't know how that's being translated, of course.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember then I entered through a door. It was a stone house then. That's how it was. Today I don't know how the house is. But I went there on 23rd. Lahi was present, then I went a second time, Nazmija was present. I understood -- I thought that this was their house. Maybe it was not their house, it could be the house of somebody else, but that's what I thought. But it was in Jablanica, that's true. So it should not be taken absolutely for true that I knew that this was their house and the staff. That was not very much important to me. Inside the house there was no sign for me to understand that this was a staff. There was not a notice saying that this was the staff of Jablanica. There was no arrow indicating that it was simply a house of Albanian character with our characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to get into a lot of detail here. Essentially there was nothing to indicate that this was the KLA staff headquarters or anything of that sort. It was a private house?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There was nothing. I did not see anything telling me that this -- in this house there was a staff or that something was being held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you see, do you recall now, did you see many soldiers of the KLA in Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just at the entrance of the village as it was the case with other villages on one side, the people -- the names of the people were taken down. So if you leave from Zhabel on the other side, on the hillside, there were some civilians. There was a shop, a makeshift shop. They had no weapons, they were sitting down. No, no, there were not many people like that that you described. At that time I thought there were not many people living in the houses; that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you entered the village somebody took your name. Was that person in uniform or just dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What entrance are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You said when you came into the village, if I recall you correctly, there was a point at which people were stopped and their names were taken?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand now. Yes, these were people -- as far as I remember, these people were armed. I don't remember them wearing uniforms. I'm not sure, but 90 per cent I could tell you that they were in civilian clothes and armed. I could tell you that since the attack on Haradinaj, it even also due to the situation before Haradinaj in Jablanica there was -- it was said that it was a cell. Serbian forces never set foot on Jablanica. Probably they tried to do that, but the local population was convinced that Jablanica was reinforced, that there were big military arsenals there. So this was the conviction of the people, local people there. Probably thought that Serbia could attack other villages but if they were brave enough, they should try to attack Jablanica. That's how people thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How many times were you in Jablanica yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there once when the meeting was held. I was then the second time, and then I was -- yes, five times. I was there five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any sign of a prison or prison -- or detention place in Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I don't want to justify or to lower the value, but there was a prison in Dubrava in autonomous province of Kosova. "Prison" is a very big word. I could not use the word "prison." There were, I don't know, houses, detention or -- I never saw a prison. I'm convinced that there was no prison. Probably there was something like a stable which could be used for something, but I don't believe that there was. You could see a prison in another place but not here. I never saw a prison there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's get out of these semantics. Let's just try to find out whether there was a place where people were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: My question very specifically and very simply was whether you saw any place where people were detained, whether you saw any such place.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't seen. I haven't seen there and in nowhere in Dukagjin Plain. Only after the establishment of the barracks following FARK arrival, we decided that a facility should be set up. This was our initiative. We thought that as the war continued we decided about setting up a facility. But then with the withdrawal of FARK forces from Prapaqan, then this idea simply vanished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you had planned to set up a place of detention at the FARK facility at Prapaqan?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we planned. The facility is there. I paid the master, I gave him the money. We thought that we set up such a facility. We thought about, you know, setting up military police, the courts, we wanted to give the trade of an army, but there in the places you're talking about, no, no, there was no such thing as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You withdrew, together with the FARK forces, on the 8th of September. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what happened to the weaponry that you and your colleagues possessed at that time?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tahir Zemaj was the commander of FARK forces. He brought an order we approved. We had weapons but we had scarce ammunition. We had received big promises but promises never materialised. We had also few livelihood. We were surrounded from all sides. The population was also gathered in certain places. We decided to withdraw as soon as possible because we were under the target, we were the target of the paramilitary Serbian forces and the Serbian police. Then we went to Strellc. We went to Mulli i Hajrizve. There we were accommodated together with the soldiers, and then we received the order from Tahir Zemaj to move on towards the highlands. So we went towards -- and dispersed in coarse highlands. Then women and children joined Tahir Zemaj. We were people with uniforms, without uniforms, we had old people with us. It was a very rugged terrain. It was highlands. So we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sir, I really must ask you to pause and listen again to the question. The question was simply this: What happened to the weaponry that you and your colleagues possessed at that time? That was the question I asked. Let me finish the question. Let me finish the question, please. Did you leave it behind in Kosovo or did you take it with you to Albania?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we left it behind in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you left it there for the Serbs to collect; yes?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left it in the highlands of Rugova, in caves. So we had no contacts. So we left it in highlands of Rugova. Everybody was looking after himself at that time. I stayed in highlands of Rugova for one month. I left Prapaqan barracks in September, but then I left Kosovo at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The point is this: These were KLA weapons but they were not left with the KLA, were they?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, these were the KLA weapons but they were not left in the hands of the KLA. As far as I remember, people took weapons with them in highlands of Rugova and then they left the weapons there with the idea that they would come back one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, if I can move on then please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be a couple of minutes then we might finish now; otherwise, we'll need a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's a little hard to predict a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it if's -- if you can't give us a solid prediction on that, I'd prefer to have the break now. We will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, we've heard that Lahi Brahimaj was occasionally referred to by the name of Maxhupi. Did you know anybody else who was referred to by the name of Maxhupi? Perhaps I can help you refresh your recollection. Did you know a man called Mustaf Bajrami, who was a commander in Shaptej?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mustaf Bajrami, but I don't know whether he was also known by the nickname of Maxhupi. As a person, Mustaf, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: On the two occasions when you went to Jabllanice to inquire about Skender Kuci, there was no sign of Lahi Brahimaj in Jabllanice at the time, was there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, I had no contact with him and he was not present. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You were asked about him being appointed as deputy commander of the Dukagjin Plain. It's correct to say, isn't it, that as far as you -- as far as your experience goes, he never functioned as a deputy commander in that region at all, did he?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last meeting in Jablanica, it's true to say that he was proposed by Rexhep Selimi that he be the commander of the operational staff of the Dukagjini Plain, but he did not gain enough votes. And in that function, Ramush Haradinaj was appointed and he was then appointed as the deputy commander. And that didn't work. From that moment, we had no other contact with his name or him. And then changes took place and another one was appointed in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were you ever aware that Lahi Brahimaj was, in fact, working with and a member of the General Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no, I did not hear that he was member of the General Staff. Later on I learned that, yes, but I wanted to say related to the General Staff that I was, myself, a member but never came to know who the other members were and never got in touch with them. That's why I called it fictitious, because it did not operate in practice; that's why I couldn't call it as a General Staff, I wouldn't call it that. And I didn't hear about Lahi Brahimaj being a member. After the war, of course I heard that he was a member of the Dukagjin region General Staff, but during my stay in that area in the region, until the moment I left, I hadn't heard that he was a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think we may be confusing two things. I'm not talking about the Dukagjin area; I'm talking about the General Staff of the UCK for the whole of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I meant that when I said that. I don't know whether he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Guy-Smith, could you give me the source you said you would need just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: May 8th, page number 3692, lines 18 through 23, I referred to small group. The exact quote, I believe, is three to five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you for it because 30 to 35 becomes 25 to 30 and three to five becomes two to three, which is not assisting the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I certainly did not intend not to assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Re, any need for re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are several matters I wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- re-examine the witness on yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One second to get the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, I'm going to ask you some questions to clarify some matters from questions asked of you by Mr. Emmerson, Mr. Guy-Smith, and Mr. Harvey. The first one I wish to ask you about is a -- some questions you answered yesterday to Mr. Emmerson in relation to the availability of anti-tank equipment and whether the KLA had anti-tank equipment. That's at 3745 of the transcript. And you'd said that there was no anti-tank equipment available. The question I want to ask you is: Did the KLA possess any anti-armour weaponry such as RPGs, that's rocket-propelled grenades?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. What you mentioned last is not a weapon used against tanks. It's a small-calibre weapon. Against tanks we had hand-held mortars in 300- and 500-millimetres, very little in quantities. We had very little ammunition for them, so I can say that the -- we had hand-held grenades which we used for 300, up to 500 metres' distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: RPGs, are they armour-piercing weapons capable of putting out of action a light armoured vehicle, such as an armoured personnel carrier, that's an APC?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's not an armour-piercing weapon. If it's used properly by a professional, it can destroy an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To clarify your last two answers, did the KLA use hand-held mortars against tanks and RPGs against tanks and APCs? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hand-held mortars were used against tanks. We had them, and they were to be used for a distance between 300 and 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how effective were they against tanks?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a hand-held mortar is used within this range, it is an effective weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was only one part of your question, wasn't it. You also were referring, Mr. Re, to RPGs?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what about the RPGs, tell us about the effectiveness of those against either tanks or APCs.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be used against the armoured vehicles but not against tanks. They are used by the -- against the infantry, against observation posts, and against the infrastructure installations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just to ensure that what you're saying is completely clear, are you saying that the KLA possessed and used RPGs? When I say "the KLA," I mean operating within the Dukadjin --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, these questions emerge from a passage in the statement that Skender Rexhahmetaj put to this witness in relation to the 23rd June minutes. If questions of this nature are to be asked in relation to that minute, then some time frame needs to be put on the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was cut off in midsentence, as I was about to say in the Dukagjin area in the period in which you there until you left in September 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I think you may have --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm happy with that as a first question but the real question that one needs to know the answer to is was there on the 23rd of June and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- what we -- let Mr. Re put his questions to the witness. Let him finish his questions first before there's any intervention, and then if there's any need for further questions we'll see whether Mr. Re puts them to the witness or you have an opportunity to do that later on. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you follow the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll repeat it, Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whatever kind of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying the KLA possessed and used RPGs, that is, the KLA in the Dukagjin area, until September, 1998, when you left?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had, but they were of a smaller calibre, 60-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To be slightly more precise, did the KLA possess those weapons around the time of the 23rd of June meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time when I withdrew, but when the FARK forces moved in, yes, there were such weapons. But there were no such weapons during the time of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 3749 or thereabouts Mr. Emmerson asked you about Exhibit P145, which is the minutes of the meeting of the 24th of June, 1998. And in response to a question from him about a military court you said there was no military court in existence at the time. In your statement of the 17th of April, 19 - sorry - 2007, paragraph which is numbered 99 but follows 106 on page 28 in the English you said: "I am not aware of any kind of disciplinary actions taken by Ramush Haradinaj against his subordinates when they had misbehaved. I know that Tahir Zemaj did take such kind of disciplinary actions against his subordinates." How was discipline enforced within the KLA around that period, and that's the period which is reflected in the minutes of the 24th of June, 1998, meeting?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tahir Zemaj as the FARK commander was stationed at Prapaqan. In the framework of the operational brigades, we had appointed a person who led the military police, who was also involved in the investigation of things. And very often Tahir took -- declared disciplinary measures against the FARK soldiers. We had the idea of forming a court, but that one never existed. I also want to add that and I said that earlier today, it -- the plan was underway to build a prison in Prapaqan. That was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I just -- if you could maybe assist by focusing on the question which relates to how the KLA enforced discipline. You've given evidence that you were a member of the JNA and you were aware of all the disciplinary measures that existed within the JNA, military courts, military police, orders, et cetera, et cetera. How did the KLA enforce discipline against its members around that period?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about one case in Prapaqan involving Tahir Zemaj, who suspended a soldier from the army. So there was that case, suspension from the ranks of the army. And he took that as a commander, that decision as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do object -- I do object to the form of the question because it presupposes a distinction. And the witness's testimony has already been that once the brigades were established, the incident he has described and the disciplinary action he has described as taken place. He's also given evidence, and the documents attest to this, that FARK and the KLA were one force by that stage and under the rubric of the KLA. So the underlying distinction that Mr. Re is seeking to pursue of one disciplinary structure within FARK and one within the KLA is simply not reflected in the witness's testimony at all. If there's a specific question to be put about disciplinary measures in a particular group within a particular subgrouping of the KLA at a particular location, then that's a fair question to put. But as matters stand the premise from which these questions are proceeding is that there were different armies and the evidence of the witness is that by the time we reach this evidence in the chronology, there weren't different armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that's the testimony of the witness is a matter of interpretation. Mr. Re, can you meet without a ruling the concerns of Mr. Emmerson? If not, I will give a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I actually hadn't finished my question. I was going to a slightly different area and I think it will meet Mr. Emmerson's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then put a complete question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from that incident at the Prapaqan barracks -- at Prapaqan involving Tahir Zemaj and the expulsion of a soldier from the army, were you aware of any disciplinary measures taken against any KLA members before you left the area in September, 1998, and I mean from the entirety of the period in which you considered yourself to be in the KLA from May to September 1998?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What disciplinary measures or -- existed within the KLA, if any, in that period?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have explained so far with things which were in the course of being shaped, but I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown or displayed Exhibit D38, which is the map on which he marked yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's several things I'd like to clarify from when you marked on this map yesterday. I'll tell you what they are before you do anything to it. The first one is the village of Maznik, the second one is the forest of chestnuts, and the third one is the shaded area or hached area in which you drew a circle. So the first thing I'd like you to do is, can you see the forest of chestnuts on that particular map?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you see the village of Maznik on that area of the map?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forest, no, but Maznik and Decan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we make the map smaller, will you be able to see the forest of chestnuts? If we zoom out, I think.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should have a look at another section of the map. It's not here. If we minimise it, maybe we can get a better look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a section which is here but not all of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think D38 is the last-marked version of this map, and I take it that unmarked, there's an earlier version, at least there's the black marking. I don't know what the size of the map was at that time. If that doesn't help us out, we either have to rely on P10 or invite the -- invite the Defence to -- I do understand that P266 is the -- and that -- yes, that should do -- is the map where only the marking of the zones appear, that is with the 1, 2, 3, and 4. If we would use that one, perhaps the witness -- or do you need this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I actually wanted to use this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another map --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If the map can't show both the forest of chestnuts and Maznik, it's not going to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the problem is the witness could not identify this before. Is there any way -- is there any dispute about where the -- these places are so that the Chamber could try to find it on the maps that are already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Maznik is straightforward and it appears, one can see it on the map, to the west of Jablanica, just outside the area of zone 3, subzone 3. Does Your Honour have it on the screen now, the top -- very top of the screen. If you see the circle around Dasinovac and the circle around Jablanica, between the two is Maznik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the witness gave evidence yesterday that he had intended to draw the black line of zone 3 to include Maznik because that village was, in fact, within subzone 3. I'm less confident about the -- the other location that Mr. Re is looking for, the forest of chestnuts. I think I know where it is, but rather than give evidence myself, that is something I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time we don't have to make a very complex exercise to hear from a witness a geographical place and we could just guide him to it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I've got no idea where the chestnuts are.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it's on the western side of the main road; in other words, it's west of the main road near Decan, but I may be wrong about that. In other words, it would be difficult to see it on this map because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: . Yes. It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- this is focusing primarily on east of the main road, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have the larger map on the ELMO so that we can use ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is a bit lost as far as the places are concerned, Mr. Re, so it would certainly assist us if you would locate the positions on the map and seek confirmation by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tetaj, could you just -- you're looking at the computer screen. Can you see the forest of chestnuts on the image which is displayed on the computer which is D38, or do you need to look at the large map which is to your right on the --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not clear, but I can put a point where it could be, where it's located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you start marking, could you explain to us approximately where you think it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you describe to us, is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a wider territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the "150." This is the quote, but Gjeravica, which is higher covers this, it's the height of 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, Now, first of all give us some guidance. I see on the map, I see, is it close to Junik, is it close to Decani, is it close to where approximately --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Close to Decan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Close to Decan. North, west, south, or east of Decan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: West of Decan, and that's a very limited area. You said it was the 150. Where do we find the 150?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Does Your Honour see the word "church"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's the 150, yes. It's close to that place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Near the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is the chestnut --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Can D38 be moved up any further? If it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the problem with D38 is that if you mark a map, then you -- for once and forever you choose the size, the zooming in and the zooming out. So if we want to have a larger map, then we have to go back to P10 because this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that the limit of the one we are seeing on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we could look at the ELMO because there we have the larger map. I see the witness is pointing at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where it is, right here. That's where the forest of chestnuts is. This is the point where I'm putting the pointer, this is where the forest of chestnuts is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
