utterances.text: The witness points at a position immediately -- immediately west from Decan where the map reads "church 2645 (150)."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think it's actually on the -- I think that can actually be seen on the map D38. It's just outside -- just to the left of the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Right here -- now it's bigger, the map is bigger right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to mark two things on this map which will then get a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So can we put it back to its original size --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least zoom out a but, perhaps not all of its original size.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just wanted to display Maznik -- that's okay. That will work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So what I want you to do is, can you mark with a black X on that map where the forest of chestnuts is. Just draw with a black X the forest of chestnuts.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you make it just a little bit larger.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the village of Maznik to the right of the screen. I just want you to -- if you need to extend the area which is subzone 3 to include Maznik, can you just draw that boundary in and put a 3 in it as well, please.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while we're still on that before --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you want to get a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I just wondered whether any further marking is needed; otherwise, we'll ask the registrar to assign a number to the -- to this map, which differs from D38 to the extent that additional black markings are made on it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P268, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just finally on this map, I just want you to clarify something about the black hached mark where you drew a blue circle around -- just to the left or west of the lake yesterday and you've drawn a blue circle within the hached black area.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that I circled it and I made a mistake, and that's why I have hached it and made the explanations yesterday because this was an area where the Serbian forces were deployed and stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are you saying that means that you didn't consider that to be within subzone 1 because the Serbian forces were there?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have it in front of your screens, it will be in this shape, and the 1 -- subzone number 1 was here, but the part of Bitesh was a very weak one and it does not belong to the subzone number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you give a time-period for when it was not part of subzone 1?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was from the start until the moment I left the Dukagjin region because it was a key position of the Serb forces, and they never left that position because it was a strategic point from where they could control villages of Dubrave, Baballoq, and Gllogjan. And from there these villages were controlled by them, Baballoq, Gramaqel, and Dubrave. Further, deeper, it was Prilep. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll finish with that particular map, thank you. This morning Mr. Guy-Smith asked you some questions about someone called Mete Krasniqi around page 15 of the transcript. And just to clarify some of the issues he raised, I just wish to take you to paragraph 27 of your statement exhibited in evidence here, that's your statement under Rule 92 ter, which is Exhibit 265. I'll just remind you of what it says and I'll ask you something. Paragraph 27 says that: "When I asked Faton Mehmetaj about what had happened to Sanja Balaj, he said she was suspected of being a spy and collaborating with the state security and the MUP and that she therefore had to be eliminated. He said that he had given the order to Mete Krasniqi to arrest and eliminate her. Later on I met with Mete Krasniqi, who confirmed to me that he had arrested and eliminated Sanja Balaj on the order of Faton Mehmetaj. Mete Krasniqi was always wearing a black MP UCK uniform, and everyone from the Baranski MUP [as interpreted] area knew that he was a member of the UCK MP," meaning military police. My question about that is: When was it that everyone was aware that he was a member of the KLA MP and was wearing a black UCK uniform?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody knew about it from the beginning until he left Kosova, he was always wearing uniform and always wearing black civilian clothes. He played the role of the military police; however, later I learned that he was accompanied was Faton Mehmetaj. However, to answer your question, from the beginning until the departure from Dukagjin, he was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just said he played the role of the military police. Can you inform the Trial Chamber what you mean by he played the role of the military police.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a car. He moved around in the places I described. He had no team. I saw him from a distance, I saw him passing. He acted like he was independent, that's the way I wanted to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What with?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had automatic weapons, to -- kind of Kalashnikov, 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Emmerson asked you about Skender Kuci and what you knew about him and the circumstances of his death. You gave evidence the day before about being present when his body was exhumed from a place in Jablanica. What was he buried in when the body was taken from the ground?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the clothes. I saw only black colour, something -- I did not see any clothes on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was the body just buried in the ground or was it buried in a coffin or in clothes or a bag? How was it buried?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was put in -- simply into the ground without coffin. He was simply put into the ground. There was nothing there, there was no coffin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, when you say you did not see any clothes on him, are you saying that he was buried naked or you don't remember or didn't notice clothes on him?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the hand and the head and the chest. I don't remember whether there was sheets. It was also at night. There was dust. I saw only the hands, chest, and head. They were in black colour and he, as I said, was buried simply into the ground without coffin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Something I want to clarify from testimony yesterday and the day before related to young men from your village going to Albania to obtain weapons. On Monday I asked you some questions, and that appears at page 26 of that day's transcript, and I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the final version we don't find the pages anymore --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have a page number? Or if you give one or two words which are typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "How did they get the weapons back ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not very typical words, but if there's any word nearby which is more typical because "weapons" might --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Inconvenient circumstances."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the others, that's page 3622.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 3622. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question I asked you was -- you were telling -- you were telling us about -- or the Trial Chamber about Ramush telling you the young people could go to Gllogjan and from there go to Albania and get weapons. And I asked you: "Did any of those young men you sent go to Gllogjan to get weapons?" And you answered: "Yes, they did." And then I asked you: "When did they go to Albania, in what circumstances? How did they get the weapons back? Where did they return to?" And you answered: "As I said earlier, there was a group of young men who we appointed from the village. They went to Gllogjan. From Gllogjan they went across the border to Albania. They stayed for a few days. They brought back some light weapons and brought them back with them in very inconvenient circumstances at the time." Now, yesterday Mr. Emmerson cross-examined you, and it was at page 24 of yesterday's transcript, and he asked you -- if I can find the consecutive-numbered one in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or a typical word will do as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Courage." "People took the courage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- yes, line 14. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson asked you about your contacts with Mr. Haradinaj, and he asked you whether Ramush was involved in how to get the weapons. And you said: "No, no, no. He was in Gllogjan. We were in contact with Albania at the time. We sent the people across the border. It was very, very risky. So these people took the courage and they went there, so it was through the contacts we had with Albania at the time." Now, I just want to take you to -- further to that to your consolidated statement of 17th of April at paragraph 24 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 39 of that statement, in which you said in relation to the meeting with Ramush Haradinaj in mid-April, 1998 after you -- and then you had gone back to your village, you said: "I was in charge of the HQ and I was to be informed if something or someone was noticed. I also selected five or ten people to go to Gllogjan in order to collect the weapons in Albania. I remember the names of the following: Afrim Tetaj, Gani Gecaj, Agron Tetaj, and Lan Gecaj. They told me afterwards that they had travelled from Gllogjan to Albania and returned with weapons -- with the weapons via Gllogjan to Donja Luka, each of them carried as many weapons as they could." I just wish to clarify the answer you gave to Mr. Emmerson in relation to your contact with Ramush Haradinaj. Are you saying that between your first meeting in about mid-April, 1998 and the meeting on the 26th of May, 1998, you didn't have any contact with Mr. Haradinaj but you sent young men to Gllogjan, and from there they went to Albania to get the weapons and then return to your village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, then through Gllogjan returning? Is that -- because that's the evidence of the witness until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure it was returning. I thought the witness said that they came straight back to his village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could not have contacts with Albania. When I mentioned Ramush, I referred to the first meeting where he suggested where we -- what we should do, what we should do to cope with weapons shortages. I mentioned Gllogjan because Gllogjan was an area through which people could pass more freely; from there they could go to Hereq, to Reka e Keqe, and then to the border. So the people passed through Gllogjan, people passed through Gllogjan. They went from there to the mountains. They were the people who were brave, who had the courage; however, they did it under very difficult circumstances. They came back through very many hardships. The border was protected by Serbian forces, so they came at night. They came on donkeys and horses with primitive ways also with big risks. They came directly to the village then back. They came directly to the village. They were tired, exhausted. They carried some light weapons. They came back after a few days. You asked me whether we had contacts with them, no, we could not have any contact with them during the time they were away, because we had no means to have such contacts. This is my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just wish to clarify something in the statement where you said at paragraph 39: "I also selected five or ten people to go to Gllogjan in order to collect the weapons from Albania." Can you -- was it Ramush Haradinaj who suggested that they go to Gllogjan in order to collect the weapons from Albania?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramush was the one who told us that they should go through Gllogjan. That was also the most logical thing to do. They had no other way to go, even if Ramush hadn't told us. That was the more accessible way for us at that moment. This is what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know whether those young men who went through Gllogjan on the way to Albania to collect weapons met Ramush Haradinaj or any of his KLA associates on their way through Gllogjan to Albania?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I have no information whether they met Ramush Haradinaj. I cannot confirm this. I was not present. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, it's still unclear. You refer to paragraph 39 of the consolidated statement. Let's try to clarify that. Mr. Tetaj, in one of the statements - and I read that to you - you say: "I remember the names of the following: Afrim Tetaj, Gani Gecaj, Agron Tetaj, and Lan Gecaj. They told me afterwards that they had travelled from Gllogjan -- "

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gani Gecaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That they had travelled from Gllogjan to Albania and returned with the weapons via Gllogjan to Donja Luka." Now you tell us that they came directly back to your village which is Donja Luka, whereas in this statement you -- the itinerary on the way back would be through Gllogjan to Donja Luka. That is not fully consistent. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I explained, I passed through the most secure way. Then they came back probably from that route -- through that route, yes, yes. But I don't know exactly. I'm not sure. I know that they brought the weapons to the destination, to the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And whether that was through Gllogjan or not, you cannot with certainty say whether or not through Gllogjan. And then for also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I'm not sure. Probably. They told me about the hardships, the difficulties, without bread, the difficult terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that they came back directly to the village is -- you're not sure about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just excuse me for one moment to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Gjukaj. No, this should not be Gjukaj here. The name should be Gani Gecaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This will all be verified. This is not the final version, Mr. Tetaj. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey asked you some questions this morning about your visit to Jablanica and you referred to a meeting there. I just want to take you to a paragraph of your statement of 17th of April, 2007, where you referred to the meeting. It's paragraph 52, and you were asked questions yesterday by Mr. Emmerson on Exhibit P142, which is the minutes of that particular meeting. At paragraph 52 of the statement you say: "The meeting was attended by Ramush Haradinaj; me; and subzone commander Sali Veseli, who was introduced by Ramush Haradinaj as a major, he used to be a captain in the JNA; Rexhep Selimi; Faton Mehmetaj; and a person called Syle," S-y-l-e, "whose family name I don't know. There were some more people attending this meeting but I do not recognise any of them and I do not know their names. All the attendees were armed and wearing military camouflage uniforms with UCK patches." My question is simply this and it relates to what they were wearing and what they were armed with. What -- you said they were wearing military camouflage uniforms. What were they armed with?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about weapons. I would like to clarify that Sali Veseli was deputy commander. At that meeting, he was elected for the first time as head of the operational staff of Dukagjin. So -- however, he came there as deputy commander. Now, as far as the weapons are concerned, somebody had a pistol. They wore uniforms. Somebody had semi-automatic weapons. There were also people who were wearing civilian clothes. I saw this person called Syle, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your statement says that they were all wearing -- all the attendees were wearing camouflage -- military camouflage uniforms. And you're saying that some were wearing civilian clothes. Which people were wearing civilian clothes or how many of them were wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were wearing in civilian clothes, these were the people who came and go. They were in civilian clothes. I didn't know who they were and what were their positions, but those were present, they were wearing military clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do forgive me. Two matters, if I may, Your Honour. First of all, and I'm entirely in Your Honours' hands on this. The witness in the markings that he's put on the map has circled an area which on our map is shown as Bitesh, Bitesh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But which shows up on the translation repeatedly as the translation of Bektesh. Now, for my part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood this to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They are. That's not a matter I need to pursue, then. Further cross-examination by Mr. Emmerson:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The second matter is this, Mr. Tetaj. Can you listen to my question before answering it because I want to put a number of matters to you to see if you can clarify something for us, so pause until I finish the question. Yesterday afternoon I asked you some questions about the time when Skender Kuci's body was dug up and about whether his body had open wounds and whether the kidney was hanging out. And you said that you saw no open wounds, that the body was intact, and that his kidney was not outside his body. Just a few moments Mr. Re for the Prosecution asked you some more questions about the state of the body and you told him that the body had been left in the earth rather than in a coffin when you dug it up. And you told him you could see the hands and the head and you said you could see the chest. And I just want to be clear. Were you able to see sufficient of the upper part of the body to know that the kidney was still inside? Could you see enough of the upper part of the body naked to be able to say that the kidney was not outside the body and that there were no open wounds in the kidney area?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Prosecutor asked me, I described the moment when it was opened. We had prepared a coffin and so we took the body and put the body into the coffin. I did not provide this description when answering Prosecutor's question, but when I -- we put the body, the body was complete. There was no damage, it was simply a dead body, and as I said, there was this dark colour on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But just to be clear, you were asked some questions about clothing and you said that the chest was bare, as I understand it. Were you able to see sufficient of the upper part of the body to know that there was no wound in the kidney area and no kidney outside the body? Could you see enough of the upper part of the body clearly to be able to express the -- or give the evidence that the body was intact in that area?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say with full responsibility that the body of Skender Kuci was complete. Now, you can ask me different questions, but the circumstances were such. But the body was complete, hands, all body parts were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Guy-Smith:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For purposes of clarity, based on a question and concern that was proposed by the Judge, I'd like to see if we can get an understanding with some precision to the best of your knowledge of two things. Is it fair to say that the number of young men in the Black Eagles was some 24 to 30 people?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, for sure. I'm sure that these were the people. Probably it could be less, I don't know exactly, but that unit had more or less this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Very well. And with regard to when young men were deployed for action, is it fair to say that it was a small group, three to five members?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Turning to another matter, if we could have --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were no more people taking part. They always were in small groups. This was due to security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have P268 marked for identification, the map, up on screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Today in a question asked of you by Mr. Re, you marked with an X the forest of chestnuts on this map. My question --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question to you is the following: Yesterday in your testimony on page 3730 you were asked the following question and you gave the following response. "And finally, this was the shelling of Gllogjan something that took place intermittently but consistently right away through from April to September" was the question. Your response was: "From April to September, yes, frequent shelling. The artillery shells of the Serb army, they fell on the meadows of Prekolluku and Irzniq. There were positions set up there" -- hold on, sir. "And the electricity circuit which was supplying electricity to the area was damaged from the forest of chestnuts." My question to you is: Is the electricity circuit that was damaged that you were referring to in your testimony of yesterday an electricity circuit that was located in the forest of chestnuts where you have placed the X?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When the put the cross was the place where they were stationed for a long time. It was a key position for the Serb forces. All along they had anti-aircraft artillery and infantry forces and ammunition, and they used the artillery from there to bomb, to shell the villages of Dubrava, Baballoq, and Gramaqel. And I said that there is a 13 and-a-half-kilometre distance, aerial distance, from there. The electricity grid started from near Decan and it passed through Irzniq and through the meadows of Aliqkaj and somewhere here the grid was cut off and all the surrounding villages were without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you mark on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking the Chamber if this is an appropriate map to use or whether we should use a new map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question is, are the details of the damage to the electricity system, are they -- what's the relevance? I mean, the Chamber is willing to accept the damage was done to the electricity supply system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if we would not know exactly which --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the Chamber's satisfied, then I'm happy not to go into the world of maps, having watched what's happened before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey, any further questions? Judge Stole has one or more questions to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: In answering one of the --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: -- questions from Mr. Guy-Smith today you stated at line -- page 24, line 2 onwards: "I would like to declare again openly I had contacts with Idriz Balaj but I never knew him as Idriz Balaj. He can confirm it himself. I knew him as Toger and I knew that he did not come from that region. His name Idriz Balaj, I read it, learned about it later." Now, in answering Mr. Re's questions about Toger or Togeri's activities in the Dukagjin area, on Monday or earlier this week you answered or you stated that you never knew that he was called Toger or Togeri at the time. Can you reconcile these answers for me?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll explain. It's the opposite. I knew the nickname of Togeri, but I did not know that Togeri was Idriz Balaj. And I learned his real name from the books that were written after the war. It was then that I learned what his real name was, where he came from. During the first meeting, Ramush Haradinaj introduced him as Togeri, and then at the time I thought it was a military rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: So when you were introduced to him by Ramush Haradinaj, he was introduced as Toger or Togeri but you didn't believe that it was a name but a rank, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed it was a military rank, and that's how I knew it all along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: In this consolidated witness statement, there is one passage that we have been coming back to a few times, it is paragraph 91, from the interview with the investigator or with the Prosecution, with OTP. Where the description of a former member of Toger's unit called Astrit Berisha from the village of Pozare told me that Toger killed every member of his unit that wanted to leave the unit in order to avoid them to talk about things they had witnessed and actions they had taken part in." Then in the next paragraph 92: "He told me they experienced terrible things when serving in Toger's unit, but he did not tell me any details," and so on. When you gave evidence here in court, you have stated, among other things, that everything bad that happened was attributed to Toger. And it seems that you do not attach any importance or have any belief in the truthfulness of this, as you have described it as hearsay evidence. Did you state -- did you make similar statements to -- during the interviews to the OTP or to the investigators, that you didn't really believe in this -- in these statements?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, other than what I have already said and I've already explained that Togeri was a name and if anything happened, if anything bad happened, the people thought Toger responsible; on the other hand, if there was something good, there was also people saying it was Toger responsible. So it was all hearsay and I have not seen anything with my own eyes. I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- I think you were asked a different question. I think you were asked if you stated that, that concern that this was only hearsay also when you first made that statement. Do you remember the question? Can you answer that question fully?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. You told us about the availability of rocket-propelled grenades, RPGs, and hand-held mortars, and you said they were not there at the time of the meeting, referring to the meeting of the 23rd of June, but once the FARK had arrived such weaponry was available. Now, could you tell us then what made those weapons available between the 23rd of June and, as the Chamber assumes, the 26th of June when the FARK at least is reported to have arrived. But if you have another date, please tell us when did this weaponry become available and how did it become available.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was related to the 23rd, but I was thinking about the arrival of Tahir Zemaj and his forces. That's when the weapons were available, were made available, and it was at -- Tahir Zemaj and his soldiers who brought these weapons to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They brought these weapons; that's how they became available. Then --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I have another question in relation to your answers as to whether you knew about a prison or a place where people were detained in Jablanica. You -- I understood your answers that you had no clue about any detention facility or even -- in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I have not seen such a thing. I didn't see that such a thing existed. People were talking about such a thing, but I went there several times and I saw nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the question was not only whether you had seen such a thing or -- but whether you knew about such a thing. Could you tell us whether you knew about such a thing or you heard about such a thing.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, there were rumours, but I did not know, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check your answer in this respect. You said you -- there were rumours. When asked about Skender Kuci, you together with Ramush Haradinaj went to Jablanica. You there gained information that Skender Kuci was abducted and that he should be immediately released. Now, tell me what is the difference between rumours and such direct knowledge of someone apparently informing you about someone being abducted, detained, and where an order has been given to release him immediately, by the way, an order which was not immediately enforced. Is that a rumour, in your view, or is that information about detention?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I was told, I thought he was detained. And we went there and Ramush said he must immediately be released. And the person we talked to accepted that, but I did not see a detention facility. I couldn't see anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When was this exactly in time, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was sometime toward the middle or the end of July when we first went there together with Ramush. It was July but I cannot remember the exact date. I'm not sure. I cannot confirm exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, who did show you where Skender Kuci was buried?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning we were in contact with Nazmi Ibrahimi, and he was very concerned about what had happened. And I explained this earlier. Then Ramiz Berisha, who was with me who was a relative of Kuci, and he said that he wanted to rebury him in the cemetery of Dubovik and Nazmi said, Yes, that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who showed you where near to the mosque Skender Kuci was buried?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were stopped at the first check-point at the entrance of Jablanica, there was some soldiers, guards. They told us, Carry on straight, and then on the right-hand side at the foot of a mountain you will see a torch being flashed and it's there that some people are waiting for you. And it was night-time. It was midnight, the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you came back to get the body of the deceased, Mr. Kuci. Is that correct? Who exactly told you that he had died and that his body could be found in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nazmi Ibrahimi told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he return any belongings of Mr. Kuci to members of his family?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that night, but later the wife of Skender Kuci told me that there was a sum of money that he was carrying in different currencies, there was a watch, a ring, and a car. And she said, If you can bring me the ring and the watch and I -- I told them -- she said that it would be exactly like bringing him to me alive. Later, together with Ramiz, the same person, I went to Jablanica - this was day-time. We met again with Nazmi Ibrahimi and he gave me the ring of Skender Kuci. As far as I remember, it was 1.600 Deutschemarks or there was some other currency as well. But it was roughly 1.600 worth of Deutschemarks and the watch, and I gave it back to Skender Kuci's wife. We asked about the car and we were told that it was damaged, and he said it is possible to return it but the car was never returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the car damaged -- were you told that the car was damaged or that it was used for other purposes?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw it myself, but I was told that it was painted in camouflage and it had participated in various military operations and it was completely destroyed. And they did not -- the family did not insist any further on getting it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you ever ask why the body of Mr. Kuci was not directly returned to his family? Why was he buried in Jablanica? Did they ever explain to you why? Where you had asked about him several times, where Mr. Haradinaj had ordered him to be immediately released, why he was buried in Jablanica, not the place, from what I understand, where he received medical care and where he died.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember asking these questions, but I knew that he was from Lutoglava near Peje. It was an area dominated by the Serb forces and there was no chance of sending him back there. So there was no chance of asking the question, Why not send him back there? And the family in the Dubovik village saw it more reasonable to bury him there, for the time -- for that time. But the will of his widow, the wish of his widow was approved so that the body should be dug up and reburied in Dubovik. Dubovik is not his home place, but it's -- there is a family connection with Dubovik. I don't know whether it's -- he is an uncle or a nephew of that family, I don't know specifically. It was a very short time we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I return to one of my earlier questions. In your consolidated statement, paragraph 82, it reads: "Nazmi Ibrahimi replied that he could not be released on that day due to his injuries caused by the prison guards who caught him when he had tried to escape from the prison. That was the first time that I heard about a prison." Again my question: Is that rumours or is that direct, concrete information about the existence of a prisons -- prison in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it, I cannot deny that, but I never saw it. With my own eyes I never saw such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is not whether you saw it with your own eyes but if these are rumours, or whether this is direct, concrete information given to you about the existence of a prison, which apparently is confirmed by what you later personally experienced in relation to the fate of Skender Kuci.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it is. This is what it was. That was what the answer was, that I cannot confirm it. I could not confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You testified today about the Black Eagles and the role they played, how welcome they were in villages in support of the defence of the villages. We also heard evidence that in some of the villages they would rather not see Toger or Togeri arrive because of his list and because he wanted to go after certain persons. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe that's what the evidence was. I think what we heard was they did not want him to arrive because there would -- he would bring the war with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think about the list, but let me just find that then before I continue. If someone could assist me with the list issue then -- to find it. I previously had it on my screen but I've forgotten to make a note. Yes, that was about the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the reference is at page 3671, lines 15 through 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If it's any assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I'm afraid I'm working from an uncorrected transcript in the sense that it's not the final pagination, but the word "welcome" and the word "target" will bring up a passage of transcript not from yesterday but from the evidence in chief given on Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- which I think is the passage that Mr. Guy-Smith has in mind and that I remember it was in answer to a specific question from Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to find the word "welcome" on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's the first -- I'm sorry, the second reference to welcome, to the word "welcome" on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's on 3676.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I also refer you to 3673, which is where the notebook evidence came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson was correct, it was the 3676 reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I found that, yes. Yes. Perhaps we should be a bit more precise, Mr. Tetaj, on that part of your testimony. You were asked about the list and whether there were people wanted on that list. And -- and you said on the question, Were there villages in the third and fourth subzone in which Toger and his unit were not allowed access, you said: "Yes, it's true, especially in Isniq [Realtime transcript read in error "Irzniq"] and in Bistrica" --

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isniq.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "There were some people for whom Toger was not very welcome so he is not welcome to go to these places. This happened because they were afraid -- because they thought that if the Toger would come and the Serb forces would come later and then the population would become a target." Next question was: "Were Toger and his men entering villages looking for people who were wanted?" The answer was: "Yes." Next question was: "Was that why villagers prevented them, tried to prevent them from entering the villages?" And then you started explaining about others. The previous commander you gave a name who was -- that there was another person before Toger. Now, that picture, whether the fear came from rumours or from facts is quite different from the picture you gave us today, which was that Toger was a welcome support when a defence was needed against the Serb forces. I'd like to hear a further explanation from you in this respect because you gave two rather different pictures.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can clarify. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were being attacked by the Serb forces, the arrival of Toger with his unit was most welcome, and that was when we were being attacked, when the Serbs were actively attacking. When there was calm, the arrival of Toger might make him visible and the Serbian forces would be attracted and would attack. In this context I meant that he was not welcome, but his assistance was okay. But that was for as long as he was not detected and followed by the Serb forces, because then the situation would become more complicated. That's what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that the civilian population would be targeted and that there was a list with wanted people, what role did that play in how welcome he was?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be clear. This was at the beginning. The lists were not drawn up by Toger. They were lists compiled by other people who wanted to compromise those on the list, and they were coming from -- they pertained to different political parties, and that was a way of compromising those opponents who they did not like. That's how I saw it. This is as far as I understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that -- in your consolidated statement that based on what you heard during the time you served in the UCK, Toger and his unit were responsible for the kidnappings and killings of Albanians, Serbs, and Romas in the Dukagjin area. Kidnappings for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I heard, these are rumours. I haven't seen them. They were -- this was the opinion of the people. I haven't seen anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement you also said the following: "However, in the villages of the third and the fourth subzone, Toger and his unit were not allowed access because the people were afraid of him. He and his unit were known for entering villages, looking for people who were wanted. That is why they had manned check-points and gates at the entrances of the villages as well. Toger and his men were known for their brutality." That is quite different from what you just said, that people would not welcome Toger because he would attract Serbian attention.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as I remember, I wanted to say exactly what I told you. The truth is what I told you, to you. I don't remember what you said. There is no case about which I could say that Toger was responsible for. I told you only about the incident in Irzniq. This -- that was the only one, but I haven't seen anything. That's what the people thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then on -- one question. Could you please look at tab 24 of the bundle that was given to you. At the very end of these minutes it reads: "Rrustem Tetaj volunteered for Reka." Could you tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about it. Reka is Reka e Keqe. I don't know what it has to do with this. And with the person Mehmet Kodra, I don't know this person either. It's not clear to me what is the reason somebody has made such a note here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There was just matter I wanted to raise with Your Honour, if I may, very briefly, and it relates to the arrival date in relation to FARK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply this: I think the evidence that we've heard so far is that there were two stages in the arrival process; in other words, arrival across the border and then arrival in this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most important for me was that where this weaponry came from, whether that was on the 26th or the 28th or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I just put one question to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examination by Mr. Emmerson:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Tetaj, that there was a period about a week or so between the time when Tahir Zemaj first crossed the border into Kosovo and the time when he took his men to the east side of the Peje-Gjakove road and up to Isniq, about a week?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, that's true. I know the house where he stayed in Prapaqan, it was a private house; yes, it's true what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And so that would put their arrival in the Isniq-Prapaqan area sometime during the first week of July?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but surely yes. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The only other matter I wanted to raise very briefly was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at page 3492, second line, you would see that the arrival in Jasic village, which seems to have been the first stop in the Dukagjin area, bears a rather precise date and that's of course not perhaps the date on which one arrived in Prapaqan.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Jasic is the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware, but it's already in the Dukagjin zone, it's close to Gllogjan, isn't it, although there are -- I must say there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- two Jasics.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because there's one --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I had in mind, but perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I think it is absolutely clear, if I may respectfully say so. It's the Jasic which is by the border that the witness is plainly -- all witnesses -- well, I can tell you why, because in the evidence of the witness that Your Honour I imagine is referring to, which would be Witness 29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- he speaks of Gjocaj, and if one looks at the route in, it goes Gjocaj, Jasic, Junik, and it was still whilst they were still in Jasic that meetings took place in Junik. And I don't think -- I entirely understand the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss it in front of the witness, and I don't think the witness -- it makes that much difference for the testimony we hear now but perhaps a matter to be clarified at a later stage. Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There was just one matter I wanted to raise if I could but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It will be very brief indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions by Judge Orie just a moment ago about lists and about some of the things that you'd said in your witness statements about lists. At paragraph 78 of your consolidated witness statement, you are recorded as having said: "These lists were circulated amongst the UCK village guards in specific villages that were sympathising with the UCK. The guard -- the guards had to check the identities of the persons who were travelling through their villages and to refuse access to the ones whose names were mentioned on the lists. The purpose of the procedure was to compromise or discredit the mentioned people." Can I understand the position. Was there a time when guards were being issued with lists of people who were considered potentially suspect and who were simply to be refused access to villages where there was a concentration of KLA soldiers because their entry would be considered a risk to security? Is that the situation that we're to understand?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such a thing. There were lists given to the guards, as far as I remember. This, yes, could be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If I might, Your Honour, on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have very limited time on the tape so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page 69, the last line it says: "Yes, it's true especially in Irzniq and Bistrica" and I'm not sure if it's Irzniq or Isniq and I'm pretty sure that based on his previous evidence it would be Isniq. I want to make sure, because it is a kind of detail that would be of importance at some point in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Um.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I'm happy to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Further cross-examination by Mr. Guy-Smith:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mentioned with regard to the villages in the third and fourth subzones the names of two villages. Could you please tell the Chamber what those two villages are?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two villages, Irzniq and Isniq. Then there is largaz [as interpreted] about -- they are 7 kilometres from one another. Irzniq is on one side of Bistrica river and the other one is on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were you referring in your answer to Irzniq or Isniq when you mentioned that village and Bistrica?

utterances.speaker: RRUSTEM TETAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isniq, I meant Isniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no further questions. Mr. Harvey. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's just one thing I want to draw Your Honours' attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- will it be a question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It could for you, but if I could just direct it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time and it's too much, I take it, for interpreters, transcribers, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't wish to ask the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. One second. Then we'll consider whether we need -- still the witness, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's just in paragraph 90 of the consolidated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where he says: "I know that Togeri had a notebook in which the names of people were recorded of people he was looking for." It's a matter if Your Honours wish to take it up. And secondly, I just draw Your Honours' attention to the fact that the consolidated witness statement of the 17th of April is in Albanian and the witness has signed it in Albanian and in English and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question becomes whether it finally should become part of the evidence, but we don't have to discuss this in the presence of the witness. Mr. Tetaj, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again. We stand adjourned until 25 minutes past 1.00 and we'll deal with a few procedural matters in the remaining 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I would like to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has understood that in reducing the list of MFI-pending exhibits that the parties are not fully prepared yet for Andjelkovic. One of the other large portions that could be easily reduced is -- are the -- if I could say so, the Zyrapi exhibits. And the Chamber would like to be informed without discussing it at this moment whether and in respect of which exhibits there are objections and perhaps to have in one word what the type of objection is so we can prepare for it and focus our discussions on the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with full understanding, at least with some understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In one word, it will -- where there are objections to the Zyrapi documents it will be where the witness has been shown a document and says, I don't recognise the signature, for example. And some of the material that was shown to him but which he didn't recognise or couldn't comment on nonetheless remained in the bundle. So it's that type of issue. We've written to the Prosecution on the day that he gave evidence explaining not just the reasons but with a schedule of which ones were the subject of objection and we are waiting for a response from Mr. Di Fazio, who has been dealing with that. He hasn't responded since we wrote to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would -- if there is a possibility that -- I take it that you identified the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could communicate them informally to the Chamber this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so we can already prepare for it. And if you at the same time would be in a position to have a conversation with Mr. Di Fazio to see to what extent you could agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we can focus our discussions exclusively on those still in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I -- I'll certainly do that. May I just mention three matters so that Your Honours have them, if I may put it this way, in your in-tray without dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There are five exhibits in the cross-examination bundle used with the last witness which remain to be marked for identification, it can be done tomorrow, but I'm simply mentioning it for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Secondly, we understand that a written report has been requested from the Victims and Witnesses Service in respect of the notes that Witness 29 was sent to retrieve. And again, at some point that's an issue that will need to be revisited. We haven't received any report, but my understanding is that the Chamber's request to the VWS is that the Defence should be copied in on the report. I don't know if that's right or wrong, but that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And thirdly this: I know that Your Honours have a number of matters that you're currently deliberating upon. One is the issue of the taping of proofing sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just hand in for reading overnight copies of correspondence received from the Prosecution in respect of (redacted) -- can the transcript be redacted with that first name, please, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has this. I forwarded it to the Trial Chamber along with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to just address this, if I may, very briefly. Your Honours, there are three transcript references which will -- in order to have the significance of it clear. Can I just give them to you. 2292, line 25, in the evidence of this witness in chief, where in answer to Mr. Re he denied any involvement in the police or the armed services -- I'm sorry, I do apologise, 2256, lines 1 to 5 is the passage in which he denies any involvement in the police or the Serb forces. 2259, line 1, to 2265, line 20, is the passage where he was cross-examined by Mr. Dixon on the information that had been supplied by Mr. Re in the letter, which turned out to be inaccurate when compared with the tape. And 2292, line 25 and following, was my request at the end that Mr. Re listen to the tape of the meeting and compare it with his letter. As I say, I don't want to develop that now, but may I invite Your Honours to have, if you have a moment, to have a look at the correspondence and the transcript references because they may have a bearing on the utility of taping of proofing sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. If there's nothing else, I'd like to adjourn. Madam Registrar, tomorrow morning, Courtroom II, 9.00. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
